pr_title: endpoint slice controller: handle pods with nodes not present
pr_body:
/kind bug

The endpoint slice controller doesn't handle well the case where a Pod exist but not its Node.
There are several situations when a Pod can exist but not its Node ,commonly, this happens when the node is removed, the node can not be present for several reasons, it can be temporary or permanent.
For permanent situation, there is a PodGC controller, that runs periodically and cleans up the Pods without a Node
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a1ac74224eac04dae21fcee2b32f8e914111ec9f/pkg/controller/podgc/gc_controller.go#L42-L48
For temporal situations, we should check when the Node is back and sync the corresponding services.




```release-note
endpoint slices: skip Pods associated to Nodes that are not present in the API.
```

Fixes: #107927

issue_context.title: EndpointSlice controller sync fails when Node is not found
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

The following appears in EndpointSlice controller logs when a Node specified by `pod.spec.nodeName` is not present in the Node informer cache:

```
Error syncing endpoint slices for service "example/service", retrying: Error: node: "example-123" not found.
```

This is caused by  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/baad1caee9dea68c6f9de9c14b23cfe6a96a80f8/pkg/controller/endpointslice/reconciler.go#L174-L177

Node is used to populate zone, without it, that field would be empty for a given endpoint:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/baad1caee9dea68c6f9de9c14b23cfe6a96a80f8/pkg/controller/endpointslice/utils.go#L73-L76

### What did you expect to happen?

I'm not sure. My biggest concern here is that the controller could potentially get stuck indefinitely for a single Service if one or more of the Pods was orphaned. I have not seen it get stuck indefinitely, but I have seen the controller get stuck on a Service for ~6 minutes for this reason.

None of the alternative options seem great here. Some options:

1. Drop endpoints that don't have a valid node in cache
2. Log but don't return error if node is not found, resulting in endpoints lacking a zone
3. Leave as is

With 1, we wouldn't retrigger the Service so may miss adding the node info back whenever it was available. We'd also risk dropping all endpoints if there was a bug in our Node informer cache. With 2, we would break topology hints (it bails out if one or more endpoints is missing zone) and any other implementation that relies on or expects zone to be present. With 3, we risk the controller getting stuck on a Service indefinitely if it keeps on including orphaned Pods.

So with that said, this may not be a bug, and there may not be anything better we can do here, I just wanted to open this up for broader discussion in case anyone else had run into something similar or had other approaches we could take.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Put a bogus value in `pod.spec.nodeName`.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

Applies to any running EndpointSlice controller, so likely 1.18+.


### Cloud provider

Any

### OS version

N/A

### Install tools

N/A

### Container runtime (CRI) and and version (if applicable)

N/A

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

N/A

prologue:

- There are legitimate situations where a pod may no have node assigned. An example: Before scheduling pods won't have this field set, this can go longer if the scheduler is down. Among other things I can think of that lead to this situation is node object delete (scale down) without deleting the pods assigned to it or in place node repave+replace.

- As discussed yesterday I purpose to separate the two discussions as the following: 
  - a _networking fubar_ situation where the watchers in controller manager just stopped working. I don't think controllers should be built to handle that instead we should shift focus to go-client/api-server relationship. The simplest workaround is to have api-server spitting a keep-alive style responses on when `time-since-last-event > interval`. think of a watch event that looks like `{}` that go client observes and does not bubble up to call back hooks.  Then maybe go-client later can surface `OnDeadWatch()` similar to `OnAdd(), OnUpdate(), OnDelete()` hooks allowing controllers to make informed decisions to either panic and bailout completely or restart the watch sequence. Whatever the approach we shouldn't do stuff like each controller relying on time since last updated or other means, it will get complicated, opinionated and rather redundant quickly.  
  -   A logical error such as the one described by @robscott above. e.g., a controller that has multi dependency (node, pods, endpoints) where one or more of the needed objects are not in cache, or not set by another controller.



Having the above in mind means that this situation should (or rather would happen) *if and only if* scheduler is down, or watcher are racy and we are yet to see the node in our lister cache (second entry above). It is entirely legitimate that two watchers originating from same client hit two different api-servers servers, one of which is over burdened by other clients.  fwiw if the node is not in controller manager shared cache then it also means that node related controllers don't see it as well, something to consider when thinking about that. Keep in mind that controller manager is all or none, meaning either all controllers run or none at all (because lead lease is held by another instance).

That leaves us with:
1. There is no node assigned yet to pod (`pod.Spec.NodeName == ""`) => does not matter because pod will not have IPs.
2. There is a node assigned but we can not find it in lister => 
 --> Pod GC will eventually collect these pod. if the entire CM is down then the entire cluster is influx state of partially broken. if GC does not kick in then these pods will blackhole all traffic going to them anyway (client side retrials helps here).
 --> Node will eventually show up => we should re-queue the pod for later reconciliation. and maybe log if failed to find node for x reconciliation attempts. But we will have always retry it until pod disappears or node appears.

All controllers are out of date.  Kube is a distributed system, you are downstream of the truth, and you can never see the truth as it is now, only the truth as it was some time in the past (which for various reasons may be much much more than seconds).

> I'd actually gone down a very similar path for other forms of error handling previously, but yeah, the possibility of an infinite backoff/sync loop due to invalid data is not ideal.

In general, you ALWAYS need to retry everything when you are "downstream of the truth" situation forever.  Reconcile means "I'm not in charge, I just need to do my best to converge to the desired state as efficiently as possible".  A replication controller, attempting to create a pod in a namespace that has a full pod quota, must retry forever.  It does that efficiently by backing off, but retry forever is a valid strategy.  It's important never to "give up" unless your domain model allows "giving up" (scheduling can't give up, but the node can end a pod's life with a single patch command, but as a consequence EVERY client that reacts to pods has to deal with the fact that a pod could be killed at any time).  

> It feels like a race condition, and I wouldn't have thought much of it until I saw a related incident. It seems like it can be triggered in a cluster with a sufficient combination of node and pod churn, which is very possible during a scale up or down. 

It's worse.  There is no ordering you can assume between multiple clients, of any distributed system, ever, that isn't provided by the distributed system.  Also, because anything can be delayed forever (which includes watches, informers, processes, CPUs, etc) the best you can do is converge.  Kube's model tricks you into believing these things don't happen, but they do (we've discussed injecting arbitrary 10-15s delays in watches in production to help people realize this and unbreak their controllers.

> if we know that a Node has been deleted, we know that the pods referencing that node will eventually disappear and they are invalid

Unfortunately no client can ever really guarantee this.  You just have to work with the data you have, and if new data comes in, efficiently incorporate that data and react.  If your three caches say "this pod doesn't have an endpoint" at the current time you look at the caches, don't show the endpoint.  It's another components responsibility to handle the invariants of deleting the pod or deleting the node (sometimes it's a human, who can take O(months) to solve it).  You should just focus on treating the data you have as truth, minimizing the cost of reacting, and *occasionally* we put in affordances that make ourselves less choppy (i.e. we smooth out certain transient flips, or anticipate that if we see X we should see Y in a few seconds, so we retry looking for Y a bit more aggressively).

Your controller should as much as possible be designed to "take events from your different sources and trigger reconciliation if any of them have changed".  I.e., if you have Pods, Nodes, and Services as input, you want to make your reconciliation being a function like "given current state of this (pod,node,service), check what the correct output is", and have each event trigger that function.  Making that fast is a challenge, but it's much much easier to test in isolation.

>  It is entirely legitimate that two watchers originating from same client hit two different api-servers servers, one of which is over burdened by other clients. 

since https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/105490 all watchers from the same client use the same TCP connection, they can not hit different api servers if they are using http2 (that is the default)

Thanks for the great discussion here! I agree with @smarterclayton and @khenidak on all points, especially that this could be triggered for a wide variety of reasons, and that the EndpointSlice controller should likely retry indefinitely. It can use the same exponential backoff, just without a retry limit.

What I'm stuck on is how we handle the partially valid state in the meantime. Even if we retried indefinitely, invalid data would prevent the controller from updating slices for the associated Service with the current state. It seems plausible that by the time one `pod.spec.nodeName` was resolved, another Pod for the same Service could end up with the same problem. Or some other failure in the system, or intentional misconfiguration, could lead to unexpected/invalid references.

So when we get invalid data, or references that we can't resolve, we should always trigger a retry, but it seems like we should also do one of the following so we're not blocking updates forever:

1. Drop endpoints that have a missing node, as long as we're leaving a portion of endpoints in place. We would need to guard against invalid data causing us to drop all endpoints, this seems rather error prone though.
2. Drop node information from endpoints wherever we can't resolve it. I think this is the cleanest and simplest solution, as shown by @aojea in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107927#issuecomment-1028781396. 

With that said, both of the above options come with the potential to introduce new bugs, so open to alternatives here.

@robscott the controller must get actual state of the system to the desired state of the system. We can make some sane assumptions e.g. if lost the entire desired state we can assume that something is up and wait a little (i think Tim described something similar in our discussion). But that does not apply on partial state because we simple don't know what happened and we can not tell for sure that last applied desired state is still valid. with this in mind: Pod that has no node is _invalid_ in endpoint list, so it must be dropped from endpoint list. 

IOW let us shift the discussion to "what is a valid pod for an endpoint, it must have an IP, ready (optional with override readiness settings in svc), have a node in our _local node list_, what else? Once we have that, we can make an assumptions such as pods that are invalid because they don't have IP/node assigned then it is likely that they will shortly hence retry them on short interval.

pod garbage collection does not happen immediately - it will only run the when [threshold is reached](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/podgc/gc_controller.go#L189-L209) -  `terminatedPodThreshold`. This defaults to `12500` in kube-controller-manager today. Pod GC will also happen for pods bound to a node object which no longer exists, so called "orphaned pods" [xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/podgc/gc_controller.go#L213-L242).
